article.title: The polls are close, but that doesn’t mean the results will be
article.subtitle: A normal polling error in either direction could give either candidate a decisive victory.

extraction.summary: Written two days before the 2024 election, the article argues that a race that is close in the polls can still end in a lopsided result, because a normal polling error in either direction would sweep the battleground states. The Silver Bulletin presidential model's national popular vote forecast (Harris +2.1) is built from state-by-state estimates rather than national polls, and its standard deviation of 3.1 points is mostly based on national polling accuracy since 1936. Applying a uniform 3.1-point error to the swing states, or repeating the state-level errors of 2012, 2016 and 2020, produces decisive wins for one side or the other. A footnote describes the simulation's three error components: a national uniform swing, state-specific idiosyncratic error, and demographic/geographic error terms. A regional scenario table that zeroes out the national swing shows how Harris's win probability responds to 3.1-point regional errors. The post is marked paid, but the text appears complete.

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model's projection of the national popular vote is formulated mostly from its state-by-state estimates rather than from national polls. As a result it can diverge from the national polling average.

quantities.name: National polling average margin
quantities.context: Nov 3, 2024; described as 'about 1 point' in the main text

findings.rationale: Strong state polls in usually non-competitive states (e.g., Iowa) pull the state-built national estimate toward Harris.
findings.evidence_quote: Rather, it's formulated from our state-by-state estimates.

findings.statement: As of Nov 3, 2024, 43 states had at least one poll meeting Silver Bulletin standards for inclusion in the presidential model.

quantities.name: States with at least one qualifying poll

findings.evidence_quote: We're up to 43 states with at least one poll that meets our standards.

findings.statement: The 2024 Silver Bulletin forecast of the national popular vote margin had a standard deviation of 3.1 points on the eve of the election. This value is mostly based on the historical accuracy of national polls in elections since 1936.

quantities.name: Standard deviation of popular vote margin forecast
Start year of historical polling accuracy data

findings.rationale: The uncertainty is calibrated to the empirical history of national polling error.
findings.evidence_quote: it has a standard deviation of 3.1 points. That number is mostly based on how accurate — or inaccurate — national polls have been in elections since 1936.

findings.statement: A 'normal' polling error is defined as one within one standard deviation (3.1 points) of the forecast, which should happen about two-thirds of the time. On Nov 3, 2024 that meant a range of about Harris +5 to Trump +1 in the popular vote.
findings.rationale: Such errors are in the thick part of the distribution rather than in the tails.
findings.evidence_quote: The actual result should fall within one standard deviation of our forecast about two-thirds of the time

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin presidential model's simulations include essentially three types of error. The first is a national error applied as a uniform swing. The second is state-specific error from states behaving idiosyncratically. The third is a series of demographic and geographic error terms, for example Trump overperforming in states with more Hispanics, or Harris overperforming in dense urban areas.
findings.rationale: Polling error does not move the same way in every state; correlated demographic and regional errors matter.
findings.evidence_quote: we calculate essentially three types of error: national error following a uniform swing, state-specific error based on individual states behaving idiosyncratically, and a series of demographic and geographic error terms

findings.statement: The model's simulations allow correlated regional polling errors, so that in some simulations Harris outperforms her polls in the Midwest while in others Trump overachieves in the Northeast.
findings.rationale: Errors are often regional, as in 2016.
findings.evidence_quote: We account for these possibilities in our forecast. In some simulations, Harris outperforms her polls in the Midwest, while in others Trump overachieves in the Northeast.

findings.statement: For the regional scenario analysis, the analysts used four regions (Northeast, West, South, Midwest) defined at the county level, so some states are split across regions. Each region was assigned a 3.1-point error toward D, a 3.1-point error toward R, or no error (N), giving 81 combinations, and the national uniform swing was zeroed out.
findings.rationale: Zeroing the swing isolates the effect of regional swings when there is no uniform polling error.
findings.evidence_quote: For purposes of this exercise, we zeroed out the national swing, since our goal is to see the effect of regional swings if there isn't a uniform polling error.

findings.statement: In the regional scenario table, Harris's Electoral College win probability was 96.1% (311 average EVs) with D errors in all four regions. With D errors in the Northeast, West and South and no error in the Midwest it was 88.5% (300 EVs). With a Midwest R error and the other three regions D it was 72.5% (284 EVs). With no errors anywhere (D, N, N, N) it was 61.9% (273 EVs).

With the national swing zeroed out, a 3.1-point Harris overperformance in the Midwest alone gives her a 69% chance of winning. A Midwest overperformance combined with Trump overperforming in the South and West gives her 36%.

quantities.name: Harris win prob, Midwest D only
Harris win prob, Midwest D with South and West R

findings.rationale: The Midwest D scenario gives Harris a good chance of carrying all three Blue Wall states.
findings.evidence_quote: If Harris overperforms in the Midwest but the polls are accurate elsewhere, she has a 69 percent chance of winning the race.

findings.statement: Because the race was so close, applying a uniform 3.1-point polling error flips every swing state to one side. A Trump-favoring error puts him ahead in all 7 by at least 2 points and wins him 312 EVs. A Harris-favoring error wins her all 7, with a smallest margin of 0.7 points in Arizona, and 319 EVs.
findings.evidence_quote: A normal polling error of 3.1 points in his favor would put him ahead in all 7 by at least two points. He'd win 312 electoral votes.

findings.statement: The direction of polling error is treated as essentially unpredictable in advance. Past errors (2016 and 2020 underestimating Trump) are not used to predict the direction of error in 2024.
findings.rationale: Two elections is a small sample, polls underestimated Obama in 2012, and pollsters have worked to correct their methods.
findings.evidence_quote: past error really won't tell you much about how things will go this year. Two is a small sample size

findings.statement: Applying past state-level polling errors (data from the New York Times) to the 2024 swing-state averages gives three different maps. Under 2020 errors, Trump leads by AZ +4.4, GA +2.3, MI +4.0, NV +3.4, NC +4.1, PA +4.4, WI +8.1. Under 2016 errors, the margins are AZ +3.4, GA +3.3, MI +2.0, NV -0.1, NC +7.1, PA +5.4, WI +4.1. Under 2012 errors, they are AZ +2.9, GA -0.7, MI -6.0, NV -3.6, NC +0.1, PA -0.6, WI -3.9. Positive values indicate a Republican advantage.
Herding (pollsters publishing only results that match the consensus) may raise the risk of a systematic polling error.
findings.evidence_quote: a systematic polling error is always possible, perhaps especially if you think pollsters are herding

findings.statement: A tossup forecast does not imply a close result. Readers are advised to embrace uncertainty and not to be surprised if state winners don't follow the current polling averages.
findings.evidence_quote: Either candidate could win and with a normal polling error, either candidate could win by a lot.

political_insights.insight: Polling errors are often regional. In 2016 the polls were fairly accurate in the West, while the big misses came east of the Mississippi, especially in the Upper Midwest.
political_insights.evidence: A 2016 shift map from Obama 2012 to Clinton
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Model correlated regional and demographic error terms, not only a uniform national swing.

political_insights.insight: In the 2022 midterms, polls were biased toward Republicans in competitive races in Arizona and Pennsylvania but were slightly too favorable to Democrats overall.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: State-level error can diverge in sign from the national error.

political_insights.insight: In today's polarized environment, about 319 electoral votes from a sweep of the swing states is what passes for a landslide.
The direction of polling misses has alternated: polls underestimated Obama in 2012 and Trump in 2016 and 2020.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Do not build in a directional bias based on recent cycles.

references.description: New York Times data on historical state polling errors
Silver Bulletin piece on pollsters herding

open_questions: Exact variances of, and correlation structure among, the national, state and demographic/geographic error components
Full list of the demographic and geographic error terms used in the simulations
How the 3.1-point SD translates into the state-level SD, and whether fat-tailed distributions are used
How state estimates are aggregated into the national popular vote projection (turnout weighting)
Exact county-level definitions of the four regions
